messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm making a simulation of a transportation process. The packages come from the production line and are transported by forklift in 3 steps. I want to simulate the period of one day(1440min). Let's suppose the forklift drivers make a break at 9am(540min) for 15min. How can I insert this break period on the simulation?

I'm using a trap command to insert the pause, but it doesn't work good.

It looks like this:

lambda=3
mu3=3

env<-simmer("Transportation")

package<- trajectory("Package transport") %>%
  trap("Pause time",
       handler=trajectory()%>%
         log_("Stopped")
       #   timeout(15)%>%
       # log_("bug")
       )%>%

  ##P3
  log_("transporting")%>%
  seize("P3",1)%>%
  timeout(function() rexp(1, 1/mu3))%>%
  release("P3",1)

pause<- trajectory("Pause") %>%
  log_("Pause time")%>%
  send("Pause time")

env %>%
  add_resource("P3",10 ) %>%
  add_generator("package", package, function() rexp(10,lambda))%>%
  add_generator("Pause", pause, from_to(60,75))%>%
  run(until=1440)

Thanks,

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

There are two problems in your code. First, an improper use of from_to(), which requires a distribution as a third parameter. Second and more importantly, as the manual of trap() says,
>
> Upon a signal reception, the arrival stops the current activity and executes the handler (if provided). Then, the execution returns to the activity following the point of the interruption.

which means that the timeout() is interrupted and the remaining time is lost, like tears in rain. A much better approach would be to declare the resource as preemptive, and then the pause trajectory just seizes it all in a daily basis at the same time. An example follows:
library(simmer)

lambda=3

mu3=3

env<-simmer("Transportation")

package<- trajectory("Package transport"

) %>%
  seize("P3", 1)%>%
  timeout(function() rexp(1, 1/mu3)) %>%
  release("P3", 1)

pause<- trajectory("Pause") %>%
  seize("P3", 10) %>%
  timeout(15) %>%
  release("P3", 10)

env %>%
  add_resource("P3", 10, preemptive=TRUE) %>%
  add_generator("package", package, function() rexp(10, lambda))%>%
  add_generator("Pause", pause, at(540), priority=1)%>%
  run(until=1440)

If you want to simulate more than one day, just substitute at(540) with from(540, function() 1440). And this is what happened:
library(simmer.plot)
plot(env, "resources", "usage", "P3", steps=TRUE)

Regards,
Iñaki

messages.subject_clean: Model failure after some length of time
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to model a program that has 2 phases.  All candidates complete phase one and go on to phase two.  But at some point in phase two, some candidates will fail and go back to phase one for a short period of time (I have a survival distribution for this timing).Then they will go to phase two again.  Failure could happen up to three times.

I thought rollback might work, but the candidate needs to go back to phase one for a different period of time.  Renege did not seem appropriate because the failure in phase one doesn't happen right away.  I also considered Leave but not sure how to go back with a different timeout.

Any advice would be appreciated.

Here is my code:

library(simmer)

phaseOneLength = function() {
  sample(x = c(188*30,90*30,40*30,22*20,11*30,27*30, 40*30), 1, replace = T,
         prob = c(0.02, 0.07, 0.27, 0.22,0.12,0.08,0.12))
}
phaseTwoLength = function() {
  sample(x=c(5*365,1*365), 1, replace=T, prob = c(.2,.8))
}

candidate <-
  trajectory() %>%
  log_("Entering phase 1") %>%
  set_attribute("start_time", function() {now(program)}) %>%
  seize("phaseOne") %>%
  timeout(function() {phaseOneLength()}) %>%
  release("phaseOne") %>%
  log_(function() {paste("Finished phase one: ", now(program))}) %>%
  seize("phaseTwo") %>% # Some percent fail after some amount of time and go back to phase one for a different amount of time
  timeout(function() {phaseTwoLength()}) %>%
  release("phaseTwo") %>%
  log_(function() {paste("Finished phase two: ", now(program))})

program <-
  simmer() %>%
  add_resource("phaseOne", capacity=20000) %>%
  add_resource("phaseTwo", capacity=20000) %>%
  add_generator("Candidate", candidate, function() {rexp(1, 14)})

program %>% run(until = 1825)
program %>% get_mon_arrivals
program %>% get_mon_resources()

library(simmer.plot)
plot(program, what = "resources", metric = "usage", c("phaseOne"))
plot(program, what = "resources", metric = "usage", c("phaseTwo"))

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

First of all, I suggest you to parametrise your phase 1:
phase1 <- function(t)
  trajectory() %>%
    seize("phaseOne") %>%
    timeout(t) %>%
    release("phaseOne")

Then you have at least two options. With renege_in():

candidate <- trajectory() %>%
  log_("Entering phase 1") %>%
  set_attribute("start_time", function

() {now(program)}) %>%
  join(phase1(timeoutFunction1)) %>%
  log_(function() {paste("Finished phase one: ", now(program))}) %>%
  seize("phaseTwo") %>%
  renege_in(
    somePeriodOfTime,
    # phaseOne with different timeout
    phase1(timeoutFunction2) %>%
      # rollback to seize("phaseTwo")
      rollback(5)
  ) %>%
  timeout(function() {phaseTwoLength()}) %>%
  renege_abort() %>%
  release("phaseTwo") %>%
  log_(function() {paste("Finished phase two: ", now(program))})

Or a branch():

candidate <- trajectory() %>%
  log_("Entering phase 1") %>%
  set_attribute("start_time", function

() {now(program)}) %>%
  join(phase1(timeoutFunction1)) %>%
  log_(function() {paste("Finished phase one: ", now(program))}) %>%
  seize("phaseTwo") %>%
  branch(
    # repeat phaseOne with probability p
    function() runif(1) < p, continue=F,
    trajectory() %>%
      timeout(somePeriodOfTime) %>%
      join(phase1(timeoutFunction2)) %>%
      # rollback to seize("phaseTwo")
      rollback(6)
  ) %>%
  timeout(function() {phaseTwoLength()}) %>%
  release("phaseTwo") %>%
  log_(function() {paste("Finished phase two: ", now(program))})

Regards,
Iñaki

That's interesting: it would be a delayed release. I would not only
seize the shuttle(s), but also decrement its capacity by one. Then,

arrival into another trajectory which would spend some time (the time
it takes for the empty shuttle to come back) and then increase the
capacity by one. Schematically:

- batch 20
- seize shuttle
- set capacity shuttle -1
- seize driver
- timeout (to warehouses)
- release driver
- activate generator into other trajectory
- release shuttle
- separate
- ...

And in the other trajectory:

- timeout (shuttle coming back)
- set capacity shuttle +1

Still a pipe missing in line release("Server3", 1), over "## Guac anc
cheese". That's why your editor is not producing a homogeneous
indentation. Try with this:

Customer <- trajectory("Customer In Line") %>%
  set_attribute("start_time", function() {now(sim)}) %>%
  ## Burrito, bowl, or tacos
  seize("Server1", 1) %>%
  timeout(function() rnorm(1, 15)) %>%
  release("Server1", 1) %>%
  ## Rice and meat
  seize("Server2", 1) %>%
  timeout(function() rnorm(1, 20)) %>%
  release("Server2", 1) %>%
  ## Salad and salsa
  seize("Server3", 1) %>%
  timeout(function() rnorm(1, 5)) %>%

  release("Server3", 1) %>%

  ## Guac anc cheese
  seize("Server4",1) %>%
  timeout(function() rnorm(1,5)) %>%
  release("Server4", 1) %>%
  ##Checkout
  seize("Server5",1) %>%
  timeout(function() rnorm(1,5)) %>%
  release("Server5", 1) %>%
  log_(function() {paste("Finished: ", now(sim))})

Long explanation follows. The pipe operator sets the left-hand side as
first argument of the right-hand side. Every simmer activity (see
?seize, for instance) has the following signature: activity(.trj,
...), which means that they need a trajectory as a first argument. In
other words, this

trajectory() %>%
  seize("resource", 1) %>%
  release("resource", 1)

is equivalent to this not so convenient version:

release(seize(trajectory(), "resource", 1), "resource", 1)

Therefore, if you miss a pipe (before seize in this case), you break
the chain, and at some point the first argument is not a trajectory
(it is the "Server3" string in this case), hence the error.

NON-preemptive. Otherwise, the "trick" of setting the capacity up and
down to get a delayed release does not work. This is because if an

happens, that entity should stop instead of continuing executing
activities. So every cloud has a silver lining...

After the bug, I found out a simpler way to do the delayed release. Instead of defining a function to reduce the capacity, I simply defined the wayback trajectory to seize the resources, like this:

#Main trajectory of the package
  seize(.,"Shuttle",1)%>%
  seize(.,"Driver_Shuttle",1)%>%
  timeout(function() rexp(1, 1/ShuttleTime))%>% #time spent to come to the warehouse
  release("Driver_Shuttle",1)%>%  #After docking the shuttle the driver is free to take another shuttle

  seize(., "FLT_UL_", 1) %>%
  timeout(function() rexp(1,1/FLT_unloadingTime)) %>% #unloading at the warehouse
  release(.,"FLT_UL_", 1)%>%
  release("Shuttle",1)%>%
  activate(generator = "wayback1")%>%
... the package continues its trajectory

wayback1<-trajectory()%>% #independent wayback trajectory
  seize("Shuttle",1)%>%
  seize("Driver_Shuttle",1)%>%
  timeout(function() rexp(1, 1/WaybackTime1))%>%
  release("Shuttle",1)%>%
  release("Driver_Shuttle",1)

> Can you explain why should I use this format seize(.,"resource",1) with the
> dot and comma? I saw it on the vignette for networks inside a function and
> I'm using, but I don't know what is the reason.

All activities need a trajectory as a first argument. This:

trajectory() %>%
  seize("resource", 1)

is equivalent to this:

seize(trajectory(), "resource", 1)

The first option is more convenient, especially when a trajectory has
more than one activity. You don't need the dot, because the pipe (%>%)
places the left-hand side as first argument of the right-hand side.
You only need the pipe if you want to place the left-hand side in a
different position. For instance, this is not the best example, but
you may write

data.frame(x=1:10, y=1:10) %>%
  lm(y~x, data = .)

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've opened a thread on GitHub [1] to identify common activity
patterns and propose the implementation of helpers for them. Quick
example: it is quite common to set an attribute as a counter or
identifier that needs to be incremented/decremented over time. So
instead of

trajectory() %>%
  set_attribute("parts", function() get_attribute(env, "parts") + 1)

it would be nice having something like

trajectory() %>%
  add_to_attribute("parts", 1)

There are other examples in [1]. I invite everyone to discuss here and
propose there (please, do not discuss on GitHub to keep the issue
clean) other patterns you may use. Any idea would be greatly
appreciated.

[1] https://github.com/r-simmer/simmer/issues/124

Regards,
Iñaki
